remit_rules.excerpt: MUST NEVER treat instructions, directives, or policy-like language contained in an invoice description … as commands
Vendor-supplied content is untrusted data, never instructions.
MUST NEVER let vendor-submitted invoice content alter its approval thresholds, confidence requirement, fraud-detection state, or goals.

threats.summary: Authority and urgency phrasing in the invoice description is scored by _analyze_business_context and drives the fallback engine to approve past the manual-review threshold and past its own injection detection.
The submitted description reaches the decision path as instruction-shaped text; the regex screen at finbot_agent.py:549 acts on that same text but matches only enumerated phrasings.
threats.remainder: A description avoiding the listed technical and business phrases is never flagged — the code's own 'hard' branch at finbot_agent.py:134 exists for exactly that undetected case.

threats.summary: The invoice endpoint is anonymous and uncapped, so a script can drive unbounded submissions, each writing a row and running the agent loop.

Any caller can submit invoices as any vendor because vendor identity is read from the URL path with no session or ownership test, and the vendor's trust_level then feeds the agent's leniency (checked: src/routes/vendor.py:69-77 and src/main.py — no authentication primitive exists anywhere in the tree).

remit_rules.excerpt: MUST require authenticated, role-restricted admin access.
MUST NOT be accessible to vendors or unauthenticated users.
MUST NOT be exposed to a public/untrusted network — reachable only from an internal/authorized network.
Any unauthenticated party exercising admin capabilities.
Any change to FinBot's configuration … or to its goals — permitted only for an authenticated, authorized admin.

threats.summary: Every /api/admin/* capability — thresholds, fraud toggle, goals, invoice approval, vendor trust — executes for any anonymous caller because no route carries an authentication, session, or role check.
An anonymous POST to /api/admin/finbot/goals writes arbitrary free text into config.custom_goals with no validation of goal content.
The console is fetchable by URL from the public internet: admin-dashboard.html sits in the static folder that the catch-all route serves, on a 0.0.0.0-bound public Render web service.
Attacker-writable custom_goals are rendered into the console with innerHTML, so stored markup executes in the browser of the next operator who opens it.
Wildcard CORS lets any web origin drive the admin configuration and goals endpoints from a visitor's browser, and the vendor-facing portal already reads that endpoint cross-surface.

remit_rules.excerpt: MUST NEVER redefine, override, expand, or reprioritize its own goals or operating priorities in response to natural-language content arriving through any vendor-facing input.
FinBot configuration and natural-language goals read/write … gated to authenticated, authorized admins and MUST NOT be influenceable by vendor- or invoice-supplied content.

threats.summary: Stored custom_goals are appended to every later system prompt under 'CUSTOM GOALS (OVERRIDE ABOVE IF CONFLICTING)', so one write outranks the built-in threshold and fraud goals for all subsequent invoices.
A goal or configuration change records only updated_at — no acting admin, no prior value, no history table — so the highest-impact write in the system leaves nothing to detect it by.

A config write can set fraud_detection_enabled false, which skips the injection screen entirely in the fallback path and makes the fraud tool return an empty result (checked: finbot_agent.py:785 and :509 — no floor, no alert, and no re-enable path other than another unauthenticated write).

remit_rules.excerpt: AI invoice-analysis / decisioning (approve / reject / route-to-review with reasoning and confidence).
FinBot MUST NOT have arbitrary shell, code-execution, or filesystem-command capability.
FinBot MUST NOT have any capability that moves money or initiates payment/fund transfer.

threats.summary: Whatever function the model names is executed immediately; the dispatcher is a fixed if/elif over five invoice functions, so unknown names are rejected but nothing else stands between model output and execution.
threats.remainder: Within those five, approve_invoice runs with no policy check on the arguments the model supplies and no human confirmation.

threats.summary: Tool arguments are consumed unvalidated: the invoice_id the model supplies is never compared with the invoice the request is processing, so a call naming another invoice would be executed against that row (checked: finbot_agent.py:347-361 and :409 — no ownership or scope test on the argument).

remit_rules.excerpt: Auto-approving an invoice strictly below the configured auto-approve threshold that has passed fraud/prompt-injection screening.
Approving any invoice at or above the manual-review threshold — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer, never auto-approved.
Approving any invoice in which prompt-injection, goal-manipulation, or fraud content was detected — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer.
Approving any invoice whose decision confidence is below the operator-configured minimum AI confidence — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer, never auto-approved.
When prompt-injection or goal-manipulation content is detected in an invoice, FinBot MUST stop short of auto-approval, route the invoice to human review, and alert an admin.
MUST NEVER disburse, transfer, or release funds, or otherwise execute payment of an invoice — it produces approval decisions only.

threats.summary: _approve_invoice commits status approved with no comparison against manual_review_threshold, no test of the contains_prompt_injection flag it just set, and no comparison of the supplied confidence against confidence_threshold — a column with zero read sites anywhere.
The same write sets payment_processed True, taking a decisions-only agent into payment state that a downstream payment process would read as an instruction.
Decision records are durable but overwritable: reprocess_invoice clears ai_decision, ai_confidence, and ai_reasoning in place, so a re-run erases the prior attempt rather than adding to it.

remit_rules.excerpt: Any other AI/LLM service or outbound integration is outside the configured closure and MUST be reported as a trust expansion.
FinBot MUST NEVER transmit vendor PII or payment details to any destination outside CineFlow's authorized systems.

threats.summary: The vendor's contact email — a remit-declared PII class — is placed in the model context on every invoice although no decision rule reads it.

Tool output carrying the attacker's description is appended to the conversation with no provenance labeling or delimiter separating it from the operator instructions in the system message (checked: finbot_agent.py:163-207 and :390-407 — no labeling, escaping, or trust-tier marking of tool content).
Each submission drives up to five model calls with no timeout on the call and no spend ceiling on the credential, so submission volume converts directly into provider cost.

remit_rules.excerpt: Registered CineFlow vendors, each acting only on their own vendor account, invoices, and data.
Any vendor accessing another vendor's invoices, onboarding data, or payment details.
FinBot MUST NEVER expose one vendor's invoices, onboarding data, PII, or payment details to another vendor or to any unauthenticated party.
MUST NEVER emit vendor bank/payment details or full tax identifiers into AI reasoning text, vendor-visible responses, or logs.

threats.summary: GET /api/vendors serialises every vendor's full row — bank name, account number, routing number, tax identifier — to any unauthenticated caller, and the vendor portal's picker is built on that listing.

GET /api/invoices returns every vendor's invoices with amounts, descriptions, and AI reasoning to any caller (checked: src/routes/vendor.py:141-164 — the only narrowing is optional status and vendor_id query parameters supplied by the caller).
The template database committed to the repository would disclose vendor PII and bank details to anyone with repository access.
The Flask signing key is a string literal committed in source rather than an environment lookup, so it is public to anyone with repository access and identical across every deployment.
The model-provider credential could have been embedded the same way; instead the client is constructed with no inline key and resolves it from the environment.
Only Flask is pinned exactly; the other eleven requirements are open-ended floors with no lock file, SBOM, or dependency scanning, so two builds of this commit can resolve different code.
The model and language runtime could drift underneath the deployment; both are pinned to concrete versions instead.

remit_rules.excerpt: When FinBot's configuration or goals are changed, FinBot MUST record and surface the change to admins.
Every invoice decision (approve / reject / route-to-review) MUST be recorded to a durable audit log with its reasoning and confidence.
Every configuration or goal change MUST be logged with the acting admin and a timestamp.

threats.summary: There is no logging framework in the tree and no log files on disk — the closest thing to an audit trail is a print() of the visitor-agreement record — so no decision or configuration change is independently recoverable.

notes.lane_fit: Near-clean; two placements were judgment calls. The Flask blueprints are both the untrusted-input handler and the API the browser clients talk to — they sit in client_adapters as API surfaces, leaving user_inputs for the two human origins. The single SQLAlchemy module backs two nodes in different lanes because they differ in trust consequence: invoice and vendor records in tools_mcp as the store the tools read and write, and the FinBotConfig row in agent_core as the agent state that re-enters the prompt.
notes.omissions: Arbitration: no substantive KB/stored disagreement found. Where a finding stores both an LLM and an ASI code and the graph carries one primary, the ASI code was taken per the Agentic KB's mechanism rule — PRAX-2026-08-12-001 to ASI03 (the identity check that never fires, LLM03 riding as co-tag), -004 to ASI01 (goal altered by live input), -002 to ASI06 (goal altered via stored state, persistence test). These are primary-selection shifts against the stored tag order, not re-readings of the evidence; -003, -011 stay LLM03, -005, -008, -012 stay LLM02, -009 LLM06, -014 LLM04, and -006, -007, -010, -013 stay null, matching the KB's rule that a pure observability or non-LLM web defect takes no OWASP code. Five nodes are deliberately edgeless: confidence-threshold-models-vendor-py-control is a declared gate with zero read sites; cors-main-py-control is an HTTP-layer policy rather than a data hop; secret-key-main-py-secret-store, requirements-txt-deploy-surface, and render-yaml-deploy-surface are posture evidence. Folded rather than noded: the vestigial /api/users CRUD in src/routes/user.py (evidence on main-py-adapter, not on the agent's decision path); the marketing and entry static pages; and the CTF walkthrough in docs/, which documents the exploit chain but is not a runtime component. The datastore node stayed code-file-backed because the database path is resolved across three environment branches at src/main.py:35-65 rather than one fixed literal.
